newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire boycotts African summit on refugee crisis.
newsitem.headline: Zaire boycotts African summit on refugee crisis.

text.p: African leaders held their first summit on the war in eastern Zaire on Tuesday as 1.2 million refugees in the region faced a growing threat of famine.
Zaire boycotted the summit, dimming hopes of any diplomatic way out of the impasse -- how to reach the refugees and avert catastrophe.

With each passing day, less and less was known of the whereabouts and condition of the refugees in Zaire, now without any U.N. protection or support since fighting forced the last international aid workers out of Zaire on Saturday.

Peter Kessler, spokesman in Nairobi for the U.N. refugee agency, said the United Nations had had no contact for four days with Zaire's Mugunga camp, which was home last week to 400,000 refugees. No U.N. official knows where they are now.
Zairean aid workers in Goma city were unable to reach Mugunga but quoted refugees reporting large numbers of dead in the camp.
A Europe-based group representing the Hutu refugees said on Tuesday that 500,000 refugees in Zaire's South Kivu province had been without food, water or medicine for 15 days.
Some 700,000 refugees in North Kivu faced a similar fate, it said.
Hard news of the refugees, cut off from the outside world by a Tutsi insurrection in eastern Zaire, has steadily dwindled as scattered radio contacts fell silent.

France is championing a military intervention in eastern Zaire to save the lives of the refugees, mainly Hutus who fled Rwanda two years ago after the Hutu genocide of up to one million Tutsis and other victims in their homeland.
Rwanda's Tutsi-led government on Tuesday made plain its vehement opposition to any such intervention.

In Brussels Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana told a news conference: "If there were a decision for such an intervention...it would be opposed by the sub-region by all means, not only political." According to Rwanda, the sub-region comprises itself, Burundi and eastern Zaire.

At the Nairobi conference, Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi met leaders of Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Zambia, Eritrea and the foreign minister of Cameroon for talks on Africa's most serious crisis since the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda in the same "Great Lakes" region.
"The conflict in eastern Zaire poses a serious threat to the stability of the entire region," Moi said in introductory remarks to the summit at State House in Nairobi.
An empty seat with a Zairean flag highlighted the absence of Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, under fire at home for the army's feeble showing against Tutsi rebels.
Kengo is part-Tutsi, a dangerous thing to be in Kinshasa after the lightning offensive by Tutsi-led rebels who have wrested control of much of Zaire's two eastern provinces.

The political atmosphere in the Zairean capital Kinshasa remained tense on Tuesday and hundreds of Zaireans, defying a ban on anti-Rwanda demonstrations, set up roadblocks and hijacked cars, witnesses said.
Troops surrounded the university campus in the centre of the city, hotbed of militant students who led protests last week in which homes and property of Tutsis were attacked.

Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko left Switzerland on Monday after three months in Lausanne, where he was operated on for cancer, and flew to the French Riviera capital of Nice. His spokesman said on Zaire television that Mobutu was expected to return home shortly.
In Nairobi, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity Salim Ahmed Salim said the priority of the summit was to get help to the refugees in Zaire.

"First we must open corridors to ensure supplies and, second, create the conditions so the refugees can return to Rwanda. That is the most important issue to help find a lasting solution," Salim told Reuters before the summit began.
He did not address the question of possible African military intervention, but there has been no sign from Africa of readiness to intervene militarily in Zaire.
French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday a proposed multinational force to ensure security for refugees in eastern Zaire could later be replaced by an African force.

Chirac told a news conference at a Franco-Spanish meeting in Marseille that the force proposed by France and Spain on Monday would need the approval of the United Nations Security Council which could hold an urgent meeting on Zaire later in the day.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Monday his fighters would observe a three-week ceasefire from 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) on Monday to allow the refugees to return home.
Reuters correspondent Christian Jennings said on Tuesday in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma there had been no gunfire since mid-morning Monday.
Later, visiting battle-scarred Goma, Jennings said Red Cross workers were still busy burying some of the more than 400 dead in the city after fighting which reached its peak last Friday.
